question: Can a black hole's surface hold everything inside it?

research.claim: A black hole's entropy, the information needed to describe what fell in, is one quarter of its horizon area in Planck units (Bekenstein 1972, Hawking 1974); because no region can hold more than the black hole that would fit in it, the maximum information in a region grows with its boundary area, not its volume. The holographic principle ('t Hooft 1993, Susskind 1995) proposes that the physics inside is encoded on the boundary, made precise in AdS/CFT but unproven for our universe.
research.explanation: S = A/(4 lP^2) in natural units, so bits = A/(4 lP^2 ln 2), about 2.8 Planck areas per bit. The horizon radius is r = 2GM/c^2: 2.95 km for the Sun's mass (1.5 × 10^77 bits) and 8.9 mm for Earth's. Doubling the mass doubles the radius and quadruples the area and the bits, whereas a box of fixed-size cells twice as wide has eight times the cells. Adding matter to a region eventually forms a black hole, so the black hole of that size bounds the information.
assumptions: Bits counted as entropy divided by ln 2.
research.prediction: Any physical system's entropy is bounded by the area of a surface enclosing it, in Planck units (holographic bound).
research.falsifier: A region containing more entropy than a quarter of its boundary area in Planck units, or a black hole whose entropy does not scale with area.
limitations: Black-hole entropy has not been measured directly; it follows from theory (Hawking radiation is too faint to observe for astrophysical black holes).
The holographic principle is a conjecture of quantum gravity; it is precise in AdS/CFT, which describes a model universe unlike ours.
misconceptions: The bits are not literally written on a physical surface you could touch.
A hologram is an analogy: the film stores the scene in interference fringes.

sources.supports: Black hole entropy proportional to the number of Planck areas covering the horizon; bound on information in a region.

scene.title: Can a black hole's surface hold everything inside it?
scene.subtitle: A box twice as wide holds eight times as much. Yet a black hole twice as wide stores only four times as much. Why would its surface set the limit?
scene.why: Black holes hint at a strange rule: the most any space can hold depends on its surface, not its volume. Physicists call it the holographic principle.
scene.opening: Can a black hole's surface hold everything inside it?
scene.takeaway: Cram enough into any space and it becomes a black hole, whose bits are set by its surface. So, physicists think, the most a space can hold grows with its surface, not its volume.

beats.title: One bit
beats.body: A light switch holds one bit of information: it is either on or off. Describing anything exactly, down to every particle, takes a long list of bits. So how many bits could a space hold, at most?

beats.title: Inside and surface
beats.body: Make a box of cells twice as wide, and eight times as many fit inside. Its surface grows only four times, so the inside soon far outnumbers it. So you'd expect what's inside, not the surface, to set the limit.

beats.title: Squeezed too tight
beats.body: Crush something into less room, and the pull at its surface grows. Squeeze all of Earth to the size of a marble, and it becomes a black hole. Past its edge, the horizon, the pull is so strong not even light escapes.

beats.title: Bigger, not fuller
beats.body: Pack more and more into a space, and it too collapses into a black hole. Add even more, and it grows past the space: twice the mass, twice as wide. So, physicists think, the fullest a space can be is a black hole that just fits.

beats.title: Where do the bits go?
beats.body: Throw a book in, and every detail of it, down to its atoms, seems gone. Yet hidden detail is never seen to vanish for good, so the hole must keep it. But from outside, a black hole looks the same whatever falls in: it just grows.

beats.title: Bekenstein's link
beats.body: In Einstein's theory, a horizon's area never shrinks, like that hidden count. So in 1972 Jacob Bekenstein proposed that the area measures the count. Every book that falls in makes the horizon a little bigger.

beats.title: Hawking's count
beats.body: In 1974 Stephen Hawking found that black holes glow faintly, as if warm. For anything warm, its temperature and energy reveal how much detail it hides. For a black hole, that comes to one bit for each tiny patch of its horizon.

beats.title: Unimaginably many
beats.body: Each patch is far smaller than a proton, so a horizon holds unimaginably many. A black hole with the Sun's mass holds a 78-digit number of bits. No one has measured this: real black holes glow far too faintly to detect.

beats.title: Surface, not volume
beats.body: Twice as wide, a black hole holds four times the bits, not eight. And nothing that fits in a space holds more than the black hole that fills it. So, physicists think, it's the surface, not the inside, that sets the limit.

beats.title: Like a hologram
beats.body: A hologram is a flat film that stores a 3D scene, depth and all. Light it, and the scene appears in full depth, as if really there. Space may work alike, with everything inside it written on its edge.

beats.title: Still a 3D world
beats.body: Our world would still look and feel 3D, like a hologram's image. If this is right, space and even gravity may emerge from bits on a boundary. In some model universes this works exactly; whether ours does is still open.

questions.a: Yes, but more slowly. A box 10 cells wide holds 1,000 cells, and 600 patches cover its surface; at 100 cells wide it is a million against 60,000. So a limit set by the surface is far lower than one set by the inside, and the gap widens as the space grows.
Bits: the number of yes-or-no answers needed to pin down exactly how everything inside is arranged, down to the smallest pieces. Physicists call this count entropy.

questions.q: If black holes glow, don't they shrink?
questions.a: Yes, extremely slowly: the glow carries energy away, and the horizon's area shrinks. But the glow carries bits out with it, and in the calculations the total count, inside and out, still never goes down.

questions.q: How do we know any of this?
questions.a: From calculations, not measurements. Hawking's glow is far too faint to detect from real black holes; the count comes from combining Einstein's gravity with quantum physics, and many independent calculations agree on it.

questions.q: Does information that falls in come back out?
questions.a: Whether it comes back out in the glow is the black hole information paradox; most physicists now think it does, but how is still being worked out.
About 2.8 Planck areas. The Planck length is about 1.6 × 10^-35 m, a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton, so the patches are unimaginably fine.

questions.q: Is our universe really a hologram?
questions.a: Nobody knows. The idea is made exact in some model universes, through what is called the AdS/CFT correspondence. Whether it holds for our universe is an open question.

provenance.intro_note: A pilot made in a coding session at the owner’s request, after the WebGL short film “The Arrow of Time” by Abhishek Pradhan (github.com/abhishekpradhan/the-arrow-of-time), and rewritten after the owner’s questions about the published guide into eleven chapters that build the idea one step at a time. Each frame is rendered in high dynamic range by a small WebGL2 film engine (film/ in the repository): ray-traced bits, a cut-open box whose cells and surface patches are counted, a textured Earth with clouds and air (maps derived from Natural Earth by that film’s tools), black holes whose light is followed along its real paths around a non-spinning black hole, and a laser-lit hologram, with several motion-blurred samples a frame, then bloom, halation, a grade and grain. The captions are laid over the video as text. AI reviewers checked it with an accuracy review, a visual review, a first-time-reader test and a blind-viewer test, which it passed in three rounds (accuracy 9, first-time reader 8.5, visual 8, blind 8).
